query: For automotive exhaust catalysts, what single intervention could improve catalytic activity and durability while reducing platinum-group-metal consumption? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should hold, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Nitrogen doping of a Pt-based high-entropy alloy (HEA) automotive exhaust catalyst, where a Pt-rich shell is grown on an N-doped HEA core, will reduce overall platinum-group-metal (PGM) consumption while boosting catalytic activity and durability. Nitrogen incorporation is expected to tailor the electronic structure and promote the formation of multiple, robust metal–nitrogen bonds that stabilize the transition metals during high-temperature redox operations.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard automotive exhaust catalysts based on conventional Pt and Pt-alloy formulations that require high PGM loadings and suffer from durability issues due to metal leaching and corrosion under exhaust conditions.
generation.intervention: Synthesize an automotive catalyst by incorporating nitrogen during the preparation of a Pt-based HEA catalyst to form a nitrogen-doped core (e.g., a PtCoFeNiCu structure) with a Pt-rich surface layer.
generation.conditions: The catalyst is expected to perform under typical automotive exhaust conditions (approximately 250–800 °C with dynamic redox atmospheres, including periodic exposure to high oxygen and moisture levels), where corrosion and leaching are concerns.
generation.structural_mediator: The multiple metal–nitrogen bonds formed in the N-doped HEA core provide structural stability and optimize the adsorption energy of reaction intermediates, mediating improved reaction kinetics and corrosion resistance.
generation.mechanism: Nitrogen doping modifies the catalyst’s electronic structure, leading to a tailored adsorption energy for key intermediates in oxidation reactions. Simultaneously, the formation of robust metal–nitrogen bonds in the HEA core retards the leaching of 3d transition metals, thus enhancing durability while permitting lower platinum loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to conventional Pt-based catalysts, the nitrogen-doped Pt/HEA catalyst will exhibit higher conversion efficiencies for automotive exhaust pollutants and reduced degradation over time, all while enabling a reduction in overall PGM content.
generation.baseline: Conventional automotive exhaust catalysts made from Pt-based alloys without nitrogen doping, characterized by higher PGM consumption and susceptibility to metal leaching and performance degradation under prolonged high-temperature and redox cycling.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under typical automotive exhaust operating conditions. The effect may be less pronounced if the operating temperature, atmosphere, or catalyst synthesis scale deviates significantly from the tested conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While supporting evidence from fuel cell catalyst studies (e.g., PMC10859931) indicates benefits from nitrogen doping in Pt-based HEA systems, the magnitude of these effects for automotive exhaust catalysts remains uncertain until dedicated testing is performed.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two catalyst samples: one with a Pt-rich shell on an N-doped HEA core and a control sample with a similar Pt-based HEA structure synthesized without nitrogen doping. Operate both catalyst types under simulated automotive exhaust conditions encompassing thermal cycling (250–800 °C) and redox variations. Perform accelerated aging tests followed by evaluations of catalytic conversion efficiency and structural integrity.
measurements: Conversion rates of representative exhaust pollutants (e.g., CO, NOx, hydrocarbons)
Analysis of PGM leaching and changes in surface composition using XPS/XAS
Durability assessments via life-cycle performance metrics and post-aging TEM/XRD
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nitrogen-doped catalyst does not demonstrate statistically significant improvements in pollutant conversion efficiency, a reduction in metal leaching, and enhanced structural durability compared to the control catalyst, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
The development of Pt-based catalysts for use in fuel cells that meet performance targets of high activity, maximized stability, and low cost remains a huge challenge. Herein, we report a nitrogen (N)-doped high-entropy alloy (HEA) electrocatalyst that consists of a Pt-rich shell and a N-doped PtCoFeNiCu core on a carbon support (denoted as N–Pt/HEA/C). The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst showed a high mass activity of 1.34 A mgPt–1 at 0.9 V for the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) in rotating disk electrode (RDE) testing, which substantially outperformed commercial Pt/C and most of the other binary/ternary Pt-based catalysts. The N–Pt/HEA/C catalyst also demonstrated excellent stability in both RDE and membrane electrode assembly (MEA) testing. Using operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) measurements and theoretical calculations, we revealed that the enhanced ORR activity of N–Pt/HEA/C originated from the optimized adsorption energy of intermediates, resulting in the tailored electronic structure formed upon N-doping.
